newsitem.title: USA: Key witnesses may shun U.S. campaign fund probe.
newsitem.headline: Key witnesses may shun U.S. campaign fund probe.

text.p: The potentially explosive Senate investigation of President Bill Clinton's campaign ties to foreign money opens this week with an initial focus on whether key witnesses will testify.

Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson gavels open the long-awaited hearings on Tuesday, five months after they were expected to get under way. The airing of political dirty linen will hold Washington's attention for nearly four weeks.
One top priority is to determine whether China or other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by making large donations to Democrats in the 1996 campaign.

Among the witnesses subpoenaed are four aides close to Clinton and the Democratic Party: Harold Ickes, formerly Clinton's deputy chief of staff; Don Fowler, former Democratic National Committee co-chairman; Bruce Lindsey, a long-time Clinton confidant; and Maggie Williams, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's former chief of staff. The first witnesses will appear on Wednesday.

Despite allegations that fund-raising tactics included offering big donors perks such as White House sleepovers in the Lincoln Bedroom, the president's popularity has remained high. But the fallout may be serious for Vice President Al Gore, who aspires to the presidency. Some Republicans have called for his testimony on funds raised at a Buddhist temple event in California.
The White House has dismissed the probe as "all politics" and plans an aggressive counterassault against allegations of illegal and improper campaign fund raising in 1996.
Three figures central to the investigation are either in Asia or have pledged not to testify without immunity.

Yah Lin Trie, a former Democratic fund-raiser and Arkansas restauranteur, is believed to be in China and has said he will not return. Former Democratic National Committee fund-raiser John Huang has said he will take the Fifth Amendment for protection against self-incrimination.

Thompson has said he can conduct a successful investigation without testimony by Huang or Trie. "I think it's important that the committee lay out the facts that it can, give depth and perception, the facts that are already on the record, and paint a picture," he said on Sunday's "ABC This Week" television news programme.
Trie and Huang raised nearly $4 million from Asian American sources but the DNC has returned $1.6 million in questionable contributions raised by Huang and $645,000 donated or raised by Trie.
Another figure in the campaign funding probe, Pauline Kanchanalak, whose $560,000 donation to the Democratic Party is being examined, is thought to be in Thailand.

Democratic strategy will be to seek testimony from Republicans, particularly about allegations that Hong Kong business interests funnelled $2.2 million to a now-closed policy group affiliated with the Republican National Committee.
The chief Democrat on the investigative panel, Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, has said he wants to use the hearings to build public momentum for comprehensive campaign finance reform.

"I think we ought to lay it all out. You have foreign money. You have third-party transfers of money. You have tax-exempt organisations being misused. You have the soft money that grows to unthinkable heights in the last election," Glenn said on Sunday on NBC television's "Meet the Press."
Glenn has been granted only 24 of the 58 subpoenas he requested but he held out hopes that more would be granted by Thompson, including a subpoena of records of former RNC chairman Haley Barbour.
